```{r}
two2.t <- read.table('../2025-11-25/twosp/out2.mcmc.txt', header = TRUE)
```

Below, I subsample some of the chains, in order to reduce the autocorrelation.
I don't know why the chains exploring the prior show oscillating autocorrelation
for some parameters.

```{r}
one1.t <- one1.t[seq(from = 1, to = nrow(one1.t), by = 5),]
one2.t <- one2.t[seq(from = 1, to = nrow(one2.t), by = 10),]
two1.t <- two1.t[seq(from = 1, to = nrow(two1.t), by = 14),]
two2.t <- two2.t[seq(from = 1, to = nrow(two2.t), by = 10),]
mig0.t <- mig0.t[seq(from = 1, to = nrow(mig0.t), by = 90),]
mig0.g <- mig0.g[seq(from = 1, to = nrow(mig0.g), by = 55),]
mig1.t <- mig1.t[seq(from = 1, to = nrow(mig1.t), by = 20),]
mig2.t <- mig2.t[seq(from = 1, to = nrow(mig2.t), by = 20),]
```

# Checking convergence and merging chains
I don't show it, to save space, but I did check for tendencies and I confirm
that in all chains the burn-in was enough and no tendencies were observed.

```{r, fig.height=10, fig.width=5}
convergencePlot(one1.t, one2.t)
convergencePlot(one1.g, one2.g)
convergencePlot(two1.t, two2.t)
convergencePlot(mig1.t, mig2.t)
convergencePlot(mig1.g, mig2.g)
```

Convergence is perfect in all cases. Thus, we can consolidate the pairs
of runs.

```{r}
one.t <- rbind(one1.t, one2.t)
one.g <- rbind(one1.g, one2.g)
two.t <- rbind(two1.t, two2.t)
mig.t <- rbind(mig1.t, mig2.t)
mig.g <- rbind(mig1.g, mig2.g)
rm(one1.t, one2.t, one1.g, one2.g, two1.t, two2.t, mig1.t, mig2.t, mig1.g, mig2.g)
```

# Comparison of results produced in Garnatxa and in Thermomix
During the process of running `bpp`, it was necessary to use Garnatxa. For
consistency, both the one species model and the model with two species with
migration were run in Garnatxa, although they had been run in Thermomix as
well. In Garnatxa we took the chance to improve the priors. We had learned
that `bpp` defaults to a Gamma distributions unless told otherwise.

```{r, fig.height=10, fig.width=5}
convergencePlot(one.t, one.g)
convergencePlot(mig.t, mig.g)
convergencePlot(mig0.t, mig0.g)
```
In all plots above, the red color shows results in Thermomix and blue, in
Garnatxa.

When originally running `bpp` in Thermomix, I set up the priors (red line in
last set of plots above) to reflect the believe of populations possibly being
large, the divergence not very large, and migration potentially intense. Then,
first results had me concerned that the priors could have been too informative.
An overlap between the prior and the posterior suggests lack of power
in the data to update the prior. Therefore, I set more restrictive priors when
running the chains again in Garnatxa, to make sure the data rather than the
priors are driving the estimates. The different priors seem to have affected the
estimates of the model of two species with migration. The parameters most affected
by the priors are the migration rates, for which the data does not carry much
information, apparently. Thus, when we assume migration rate could be rampant
(red lines), population sizes become smaller and divergence deeper. In Garnatxa,
departing from a prior of very low migration, populations seem larger and
divergence shallower. Results from Garnatxa are more conservative: not having
much evidence in the sequence data to support the idea of frequent migration,
it is safe to assume there wasn't much.

The large difference in likelihood is not important. In addition to the different
priors, in Garnatxa we used several more loci than in Thermomix, which must have
also reduced the overall likelihood.

# Comparison between the two-species models with and without migration
This is an approximation to the Bayes factor with a Savage-Dickey density ratio,
following [Tomas Flouri's advice](https://github.com/Pas-Kapli/phylogenomics/wiki/Hypothesis-testing-with-BPP).
The migration parameter, $w_{XY}$, is defined as the ratio between proportion of
migrants per generation and mutation rate: $w_{XY} = \frac{m_{XY}}{\mu}$. I suppose
a fraction of migrants lower than a hundredth of the mutation rate is quite
negligible. Thus, I set 0.01 as the threshold below which migration isn't much
different from zero. The prior is $\sim Gamma(2, 100)$.

```{r}
w0 <- 0.01
prior <- pgamma(w0, shape = 2, rate = 100)
posteriorAB <- sum(mig.g$W.1..2.A..B <= w0) / nrow(mig.g)
posteriorBA <- sum(mig.g$W.2..1.B..A <= w0) / nrow(mig.g)
bfAB <- prior / posteriorAB
bfBA <- prior / posteriorBA

bfAB
bfBA
```

This means that the prior assigns an almost equal probability to a
negligible migration rate than the posterior. The Bayes factor is
insignificant.

I suspect one reason for the lack of power is the fact that genotypes
are not phased. Because genotypes were estimated from posterior
probabilities, the linkage information from the reads was lost. This is
quite unfortunate, but not easy to work around at the moment.

# Comparison between the one-species model and the two-species model
The chains for the 16 steps to get the marginal likelihood for the two-species
model were interrumpted. Thus, the average likelihood for each power beta
is not retrieved (yet). But, having between 8000 and 13000 samples of the
power posteriors, I can approximate the average likelihood myself as just
the average of the likelihoods in the chain. This is a provisional solution.

```{bash}
if [ ! -e ElnfX1.txt ]; then
   find ../2025-11-25/garnatxa/bf/onesp -name onesp.txt \
        -exec gawk '(/BFbeta/){print FILENAME "\t" $NF}' '{}' \; |
   sort > ElnfX1.txt
fi

if [ ! -e ElnfX2.txt ]; then
   find ../2025-11-25/garnatxa/bf/twoMig -name twoMig.txt \
        -exec gawk '(/BFbeta/){print FILENAME "\t" $NF}' '{}' \; |
   sort > ElnfX2.txt
fi
```

```{r}
plot(bw1$beta, bw1$ElnfX, type = 'b', col = 'darkred', xlab = 'Beta',

MarginalLogLikelihood1
MarginalLogLikelihood2
BF
```

The estimated marginal log-likelihoods suggest a very strong support for the model with
two species.

# Best model
Therefore, best model is the one with two species without migration. Let's look at
its posterior.

```{r}
library(MetBrewer)
pal <- met.brewer('Egypt', 3)
plot(c(0.0012, 0.028), c(0, 2300), type = 'n', xlab = 'Theta',
     ylab = 'Density', main = 'Two species posteriors', axes = FALSE)
axis(1, at = apply(two.t, 2, mean)[2:4])
lines(density(mig.g$theta.1.A), col = pal[1], lty = 2)
lines(density(two.t$theta.1.A), col = pal[1])
lines(density(mig.g$theta.2.B), col = pal[2], lty = 2)
lines(density(two.t$theta.2.B), col = pal[2])
lines(density(mig.g$theta.3.A.B), col = pal[3], lty = 2)
lines(density(two.t$theta.3.A.B), col = pal[3])
legend(0.02, 2000, c('C. farionis', 'C. psedofarionis', 'Ancestral', 'With migration'),
       lty = c(1, 1, 1, 2), col = c(pal, 'gray'), bty = 'n')
```

```{r}
plot(density(mig.g$tau.3.A.B), main = 'Two species posteriors', xlab = 'Tau')
lines(density(two.t$tau.3.A.B), lty = 2)
legend(0.0027, 5000, c('Without migration', 'With migration'), lty = c(1, 2), bty = 'n')
```

```{r}
u <- apply(two.t, 2, mean)[2:5]
plotAB(u[1], u[2], u[3], u[4])
```

# Conclusion
The split between the two populations may have happened 0.002583 substitutions per
site ago, which would amount to any date between 260000 years ago, if the rate of
mutations is very fast ($10^{-8}$), and 2.6 million years ago, if the rate of mutations
is very slow ($10^{-9}$). Both population have expanded since then, with *C. pseudofarionis*
being larger than *C. farionis* nowadays.

The population expansion is consistent with the observed excess of low frequency
variants inferred from the fact that Watterson estimates of diversity are higher
than Tajima's (see `2026-01-03`).
